enrichment.short_title: Appeal against care order and adoption plan for scapegoated child
key_facts: JH, aged four, was made the subject of a final care order with an adoption care plan after sustained emotional abuse and rejection by his parents, in a pattern similar to that suffered by his older half-brother D.
The justices refused repeated adjournments for psychiatric assessment of the mother and family therapy, finding that any change would take two to three years and JH's timescale could not wait.
The parents appealed on grounds including discrimination, failure to adjourn, and breach of Articles 6 and 8, but abandoned a fresh-evidence argument.
Expert and guardian evidence showed the parents remained in denial and could not acknowledge the harm JH had suffered.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of re-hearing from magistrates' final care order in favour of adoption.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the justices' care order and adoption plan were upheld.
enrichment.ratio: On an appeal by way of re-hearing from a care order, the High Court will not interfere with magistrates' refusal to adjourn for further assessment where there was cogent evidence that the parents lacked insight, meaningful change would take years incompatible with the child's welfare, and treating JH differently from his siblings was justified because he had already suffered significant harm.
legal_issues: Whether the justices should have adjourned for psychiatric assessment and family therapy
Whether differential treatment of JH compared with his siblings was discriminatory
Whether the local authority had done enough to assist the parents
Whether adoption was justified under section 1 and Article 8 of the Human Rights Act

confidence.notes: Long first-instance judgment with clear findings on each ground of appeal, statutory framework, and outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Challenge to automatic restriction directions on prison hospital transfers
key_facts: T, a prisoner with schizo-affective disorder, was transferred from prison to hospital under section 47 of the Mental Health Act 1983 and made subject to a section 49 restriction direction.
Her treating psychiatrist said she posed no risk to the public and that the restriction direction impeded treatment and rehabilitation.
The Home Office maintained its usual policy of imposing restriction directions except where transfer was within days of release and the offence did not require restrictions.
Prison and Home Office documents had incorrectly stated an earlier conditional release date, giving rise to a legitimate-expectation argument.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's policy and its application to a transferred prisoner.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed on all grounds; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: The Secretary of State's policy of routinely imposing restriction directions on prisoners transferred to hospital under section 47 is lawful because section 49 is not limited by public-protection criteria analogous to section 41; his role is not that of a sentencing court but of ensuring a lawfully imposed sentence is not wholly overridden by later medical transfer.
legal_issues: Whether the Home Secretary's restriction-direction policy is Wednesbury unreasonable or for an improper purpose
Whether adequate reasons were given for refusing to lift the restriction direction
Whether an erroneous release-date letter gave rise to a legitimate expectation
Whether Article 8 assisted the claimant

enrichment.short_title: Bankruptcy challenge to nil-value transfer of Crown bona vacantia property
key_facts: The bankrupt and his wife bought a dissolved company's freehold reversion from the Crown for £200 rather than about £6,250 because they were former shareholders.
Their daughter paid the purchase price; seven months before bankruptcy the property was transferred for nil consideration to the wife and daughter.
The trustee sought to set aside the transfer as a transaction at an undervalue under section 339.
The appellants argued a resulting trust and that the bankrupt had no beneficial interest because he never intended to retain one.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a registrar's decision setting aside a pre-bankruptcy transfer at undervalue.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the registrar's order requiring sale and reimbursement of the daughter's contribution was affirmed.
enrichment.ratio: Where former shareholders acquire bona vacantia property at a nominal discount by virtue of their status, that discount is a valuable contribution to the purchase price; payment of the cash price alone by a third party does not defeat the bankrupt's resulting beneficial interest, so a subsequent nil-value transfer can be a transaction at an undervalue under section 339.
legal_issues: Whether the bankrupt had a beneficial interest in the freehold reversion
Whether a resulting trust arose from the daughter's payment of £200 and costs
Whether shareholder status entitled the purchasers to the discount as a contribution
Whether the transfer was a transaction at an undervalue under section 339(3)

Menzies v National Bank of Kuwait SAK

enrichment.short_title: Travel insurance exclusion for jet ski personal liability claim

statutes_considered.title: Unfair Terms in Consumer Contracts Regulations 1994

key_facts: Mr South's holiday travel insurance policy excluded personal liability arising from accidents involving motorised waterborne craft.
He was seriously injured in Cyprus when a hired jet ski collided with another jet ski ridden by Mr Gardner.
Bankers, the underwriter, sought a declaration that it was not liable to indemnify Mr South.
Mr South notified the insurer very late and failed to comply with policy conditions requiring prompt written notification.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Declaratory action on policy coverage, with Mr Gardner's personal injury claim stayed pending the outcome.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration granted that Bankers was not liable; claim succeeded on exclusion, unfair-terms, and notification grounds.
enrichment.ratio: A jet ski is a motorised waterborne craft within an ordinary travel-insurance personal-liability exclusion; the exclusion is in plain intelligible language and not unfair under the 1994 Regulations, and serious late notification of the claim can defeat cover even where the unfair part of a condition-precedent clause is not binding.
legal_issues: Whether a jet ski falls within 'motorised waterborne craft'
Whether the exclusion is an unfair term under the 1994 Regulations
Whether conditions (d) and (e) on prompt notification are conditions precedent
Whether Mr South's breaches prejudiced the insurer or showed no intention to claim

enrichment.short_title: Invalid compulsory share-purchase offer after winding-up petition
key_facts: Investors in Dentons sought to exercise a compulsory buy-out under clause 12 of a shareholders' agreement after a winding-up petition was presented against AKG.
They served an offer notice proposing to pay £646,253.24 in two equal instalments rather than in full on completion.
The deputy judge held an insolvency event had occurred but that the offer notice was invalid; the investors appealed.
AKG cross-appealed, arguing presentation of a petition was not an insolvency event under clause 12.1.2.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a Part 24 trial of preliminary issues on a shareholders' agreement compulsory transfer clause.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the offer notice was invalid and the claim failed.
enrichment.ratio: Under clause 12 of a shareholders' agreement, a valid offer notice must be on terms permitting completion under clauses 12.7 and 12.8, including payment of the total consideration by banker's draft on completion; an offer providing for deferred payment cannot trigger the compulsory expropriation machinery even if an insolvency event has occurred.
legal_issues: Whether presentation of a winding-up petition was an insolvency event under clause 12.1.2
Whether clause 12.8 defines validity of an offer notice or only default completion terms
Whether an offer payable in instalments could be a valid clause 12.4 offer notice
Whether a term requiring full payment on completion should be implied

enrichment.short_title: Restitution claim for unnotified retrospective sewerage charges
key_facts: The council operated private sewerage works for former council-house owners in Letcombe Bassett but charged only those who had entered express contracts.
Mr Rowe bought his property in 1988 without any sewerage-payment covenant and received no intimation of charges for thirteen years.
In March 2001 the council demanded six years' retrospective charges, causing shock because residents reasonably believed no separate liability existed.
The proceedings began as judicial review but were treated as a trial of the private-law restitution issue by consent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review recharacterised as trial of a restitution claim for retrospective sewerage charges.
enrichment.outcome: Council held to have no legal right to arrears from April 1995 to March 2001.
enrichment.ratio: Where a supplier provides essential sewerage services over many years without indicating any intention to charge and the recipient reasonably believes no extra liability exists, there is no free acceptance and no unjust factor; a restitution claim for retrospective payment therefore fails even if the recipient obtained an incontrovertible benefit.
legal_issues: Whether the council could recover payment in restitution for unsolicited sewerage services
Whether free acceptance supplied both benefit and unjust factor
Whether the defendant should have known the supplier expected payment
Whether change of position was relevant where no unjust factor existed

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 challenge to strict-liability school attendance offence

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Court Services Act 2000

key_facts: The appellant was convicted under section 444(1) of failing to secure her child's regular school attendance, an offence of strict liability.
On appeal by case stated, she argued section 444(1) was incompatible with Article 6.2 and sought a declaration of incompatibility rather than a section 3 read-down.
Section 444(1A), inserted in 2000, creates a more serious fault-based offence requiring knowledge and lack of reasonable justification.
Existing authority including Jenkins v Howells, Crump v Gilmore, and Bath and North East Somerset Council v Warman treats section 444(1) as absolute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated on a preliminary Human Rights Act compatibility issue pending resolution of the Crown Court appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Questions answered affirmatively: section 444(1) is ECHR-compatible and section 3 reinterpretation does not arise.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6.2 regulates procedural and evidential presumptions in criminal trials rather than the substantive content of domestic offences; it does not prevent Parliament creating strict-liability offences such as section 444(1) where the prosecution retains the burden of proving the statutory elements.
legal_issues: Whether section 444(1) infringes Article 6.2 by imposing strict liability
Whether Salabiaku and Hansen permit review of strict-liability offences for proportionality
Whether a section 3 read-down or section 4 declaration is required
If engaged, whether strict liability for school attendance is justified
linked_authorities: Bath and North East Somerset Council v Warman
Helmsley v West Sussex County Council
Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v Attorney General of Hong Kong

confidence.notes: Divisional Court judgment with split reasoning on justification but unanimous outcome on Article 6.2 scope.

enrichment.short_title: Landlord failed reasonable prospect of resuming restaurant business
key_facts: Mr Zarvos sought to oppose a new tenancy of restaurant premises at Lillie Road on the ground that he intended to occupy for his own business.
He proposed a new Mediterranean restaurant and wine bar requiring about £40,000 borrowing against substantial equity in the property.
The county court judge found no reliable evidence that the bank would lend and that the business projections were unreliable.
The landlord had previously run a taverna on the premises but the case was advanced on the new Boby's Restaurant plan.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against county court determination of a preliminary issue under section 30(1)(g) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1954.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the landlord was not entitled to oppose the new tenancy.
enrichment.ratio: To succeed under section 30(1)(g), a landlord must show both a genuine intention to occupy for business purposes and, objectively, a real rather than fanciful prospect of bringing that intention about; inadequate finance and unreliable projections can defeat the second limb even where subjective intent is not positively disbelieved.
legal_issues: Whether the landlord had a genuine bona fide intention to occupy
Whether he had a reasonable prospect of financing and opening the proposed business
Whether the judge erred by focusing on £40,000 borrowing rather than reuse of existing equipment
Whether fresh evidence of a later bank loan offer should be admitted

enrichment.short_title: Detailed assessment of CFA success fee and ATE premium
key_facts: Following the Court of Appeal decision in Sarwar v Alam on CFA/ATE issues, the claimant's costs bill totalled £255,745.30 in a case with £2,250 damages.
The costs judge applied the necessary test from Home Office v Lownds and held costs were disproportionate on their face.
At a further preliminary hearing he allowed the full £62,500 ATE premium for the Court of Appeal stage and a 100% success fee.
He reduced the solicitors' Court of Appeal hourly rate from £350 to £215.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Detailed assessment preliminary hearing on CFA insurance premium, success fee, and hourly rates after interlocutory costs rulings.
enrichment.outcome: Full ATE premium and 100% success fee allowed; Court of Appeal hourly rate fixed at £215.
enrichment.ratio: In a finely balanced CFA test case, a bespoke ATE premium may be recoverable in full where cover was difficult to obtain and the risk justified it; a 100% success fee is reasonable where success was no better than evens; specialist solicitors may exceed guideline rates only on justified evidence, here £215 rather than £350 for Court of Appeal work.
legal_issues: Whether the £62,500 ATE premium was reasonable and recoverable
Effect of the 50% no-claims bonus and indemnity principle
Whether a 100% success fee was justified
What hourly rate was reasonable for Manchester solicitors on Court of Appeal work

enrichment.short_title: Prisoner informant entitled to protected witness unit placement
key_facts: A long-term prisoner provided information to the police about serious crime but was not to be called as a witness.
He claimed serious risk from other prisoners and sought accommodation in a Protected Witness Unit under Prison Service procedures.
Home Office Circular 9/1992 and its annex govern resident informants but did not address interim protection on return from police custody.
Decision-making was flawed: relevant police and CPS material was not collated promptly and he was moved without proper briefing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review seeking declaratory relief on PWU placement and the adequacy of Prison Service decision-making.
enrichment.outcome: Declarations granted that the prisoner need not have given evidence to qualify for a PWU and that he should be located in a PWU pending completion of risk enquiries.
enrichment.ratio: Where a prisoner who has provided information faces a real and continuing risk to life, the Secretary of State must act compatibly with Articles 2 and 3; failure to give evidence is not a bar to PWU placement if safety requires it, and interim protection decisions must be made before or on return to prison even where Home Office Circular 9/1992 does not cover that situation.
legal_issues: Whether Circular 9/1992 adequately provides for interim protection of returning informants
Whether a prisoner must have given or be giving evidence to enter a PWU
Whether there was a real and immediate risk engaging Articles 2 and 3
Whether PWU placement was the only reasonable interim measure
